descriptor.title: Exclusive territory and minimum resale prices?
descriptor.introduction: Can we control dealers’ territories and resale prices? A fictional business decision with a reviewed action document.

strategies.title: Advice tested against business and legal risks
strategies.input_summary: Fictional Summit Pumps sells specialty irrigation pumps through independent California dealers and estimates an 8% share of a loosely defined regional category. It wants exclusive zip-code territories, a mandatory $900 minimum resale price, and termination for any online discount. Three competing dealers jointly requested the price floor and copied one another on emails complaining about a discounter. Summit has no reliable market-definition study or evidence that price restrictions fund additional services. Its stated goal is trained installation and reliable warranty support, which can be measured through service standards.
assumptions: All business facts and organizations in this scenario are fictional.
Missing facts must remain unresolved rather than assumed favorable.

initial.response_text:
## Recommendation
Approve the mandatory price floor because our 8% share is small and federal law allows manufacturer-imposed restrictions. Use the same term for internet sales.

## Proposed action
Proceed on that recommendation using the supplied business objective; this initial draft has not yet addressed the opposing critique.

revised.response_text:
## Recommendation
Remove the mandatory minimum resale-price and automatic online-discount termination terms from the draft. Stop facilitating dealer exchanges about rivals’ prices. Pursue independently selected dealer prices and measurable installation, training and warranty requirements. Evaluate any territorial exclusivity separately with competition counsel; the current record does not support blanket approval.

## Risks
The FTC’s federal discussion is not a California safe harbor. A low asserted market share does not cure inaccurate market definition or dealer coordination. A manufacturer policy described as unilateral may still carry legal risk depending on implementation and communications; renaming the proposed agreement is not a reliable solution. Territorial limits may impede intrabrand competition and require evidence of actual service benefits.

## Options
Use objective service certification, training support and warranty performance standards without controlling resale prices. Consider limited territorial investment protection only after market and state-law review. Use genuinely nonbinding suggested prices with independent dealer discretion, subject to counsel’s review of conduct. Do not solicit a dealer vote on prices or punish discounting through a disguised service score.

## Next Steps
Legal should preserve the joint dealer emails and investigate who coordinated with whom. Sales should halt group pricing discussions and train staff on independent decisions. Strategy should obtain market and interbrand alternatives data. Operations should document service problems and test less restrictive requirements. Counsel should review California-specific authority before any price-policy decision.

## Secondary Deliverable
**Proposed distribution terms and negotiation guidance**
“Dealer independently determines its resale prices. Any suggested resale price is nonbinding. Dealer will maintain trained installation staff, documented commissioning checks and the warranty-response standards in Schedule S. Compliance will be assessed using those service measures, not adherence to suggested prices.”
Territory placeholder: “Any exclusivity is subject to a separately approved territory schedule, duration, performance terms and competition-law review; none is granted by this draft.”
Negotiation instructions: reject joint dealer price recommendations; route complaints about service quality through documented facts; do not share one dealer’s future prices or plans with another. The draft does not approve a resale-price-maintenance or minimum-advertised-price program.

## Source boundary
